newsitem.title: FRANCE: Far-right French mayor upheld on pork-free meals.
newsitem.headline: Far-right French mayor upheld on pork-free meals.

text.p: An administrative court has upheld a far-right French mayor's edict ending pork-free meals for Moslem and Jewish pupils at public school canteens in the southern French town of Marignane.

In a decision reached last week and announced on Monday, the Marseille court rejected a suit by eight Moslem and Jewish families, finding that Marignane mayor Daniel Simonpieri was justified in ending the special meals as a money-saving measure.
Separately, the administrative court prevented Marignane from imposing a second rule that would have limited access to school canteens to children with two working parents.
A parents organisation had argued in that case that the regulation would keep out the poorest students, those whose parents were unemployed and were most in need of a good meal.
Simonpieri is one of three members of the extreme-right National Front party who won control of a French city hall in last year's nationwide municipal elections.

The front is fiercely anti-immigration, arguing that jobs and national benefits should be reserved only for native-born citizens, but it insists that it is not anti-Arab nor anti-semitic. Marignane has a relatively large North African Moslem Arab minority.
The move to end pork-free meals at Marignane schools, which took effect in September, had been attacked by the eight families as discriminatory.

Commissioner Gerard Ferulla, representing the state, acknowledged during a hearing on the case that students had the right to follow their religious beliefs in schools but argued that the right was "not without limits".

Attorney Ronald Perdomo, representing the town of Marignane, argued in a memorandum that "Jewish and Moslem students have no more right to meals without pork than do Catholic students to demand meals of fish on Fridays".

In a related case, the French Education Ministry confirmed that a Paris teacher had asked Education Minister Francois Bayrou to arbitrate her refusal to teach a young high school student who wears an Islamic scarf to classes.

A spokeswoman said Bayrou would have no public statement on the request by teacher Marie-Pierre Lombardo that he determine whether she can continue to refuse to teach maths to a Moslem girl student identified only as Loubna.

Lombardo, a member of a left-wing union which backs secularism in schools, said she cannot teach Loubna as a matter of conscience because the scarf is a religious emblem that violates her lay principles.
